cards.title: Why One Cluster Is Never Enough
cards.teaser: A single Kubernetes cluster is a single blast radius. One misconfigured admission webhook, one runaway workload, or one availability-zone outage can take every tenant down simultaneously. Understanding the limits of a single cluster is the starting point for multi-cluster architecture.

runs.text: The four forces that push organisations toward multiple clusters:

items.text: A rogue DaemonSet consuming all CPU on every node, a broken webhook that blocks every admission, or an etcd corruption event affects all workloads in a single cluster. Splitting tenants or criticality tiers across clusters limits the scope of any single failure.

Latency-sensitive workloads need a cluster near the users they serve. Active-active multi-region setups require independent clusters per region, because a single cluster spanning regions cannot survive a network partition without split-brain problems.

GDPR, HIPAA, and financial regulations often require data to remain within specific legal jurisdictions. A US cluster and an EU cluster managed independently are cleaner to audit than one cluster with namespace-level controls that regulators have to trust.

Large enterprises running hundreds of microservices owned by different teams find namespace-per-team sharing increasingly fragile: noisy-neighbour resource contention, accidental service-discovery cross-talk, and different upgrade cadences for different teams all push toward cluster-per-team or cluster-per-platform-tier models.

runs.text: The counter-pressure is operational overhead: every additional cluster is a new control plane to upgrade, a new certificate rotation to track, and a new audit trail to maintain. The right cluster count is the minimum that satisfies the isolation and geographic requirements — not one cluster per team by default.

Shopify, Airbnb, and most large cloud-native companies run 10–100+ clusters in production. GitOps tooling (ArgoCD, Flux) was built precisely to manage that fleet without per-cluster manual intervention.

One cluster means one failure domain, one regulatory boundary, and one noisy-neighbour pool. Multiple clusters trade operational complexity for isolation — blast radius shrinks, regions become independent, and tenants cannot interfere with each other.

cards.title: Cluster Federation: KubeFed and Its Limits
cards.teaser: Cluster federation promised a single control plane to manage many clusters. KubeFed v1 shipped with Kubernetes 1.3; v2 (kubefedctl) followed years later. Both saw limited real-world adoption. Understanding why explains the architecture choices GitOps tools made instead.

runs.text: ) aimed to let a single API server propagate workloads and services to member clusters. The v1 design (2016) used a federated API server that accepted standard Kubernetes resources and fanned them out. In practice it proved brittle:

items.text: A federated Deployment needed to express overrides per target cluster (different replica counts, different image tags). The override specification was verbose and hard to compose.
Every new Kubernetes resource type required a new federation shim. CRD proliferation made keeping federation in sync with core Kubernetes nearly impossible.
Availability of the federation control plane itself.
The entity that was supposed to provide high-availability became a single point of failure for all member clusters.

runs.text: KubeFed v2 (2019) moved to a CRD-based model:
and similar types replaced the mirrored API. This reduced the upstream-coupling problem but introduced its own complexity: operators had to learn a parallel object hierarchy. Adoption remained low.
In 2023, the KubeFed project was archived. The community conclusion: federation at the API layer adds complexity without proportionate benefit. The winning pattern instead is
— each cluster has its own GitOps agent that reconciles independently from a Git source of truth, with no single federation control plane.

If you encounter legacy infrastructure using KubeFed v1 or v2, plan to migrate. The project is archived and receives no security patches. GitOps-based fleet management (ArgoCD ApplicationSets, Flux multi-cluster) is the supported replacement pattern.
KubeFed tried to put all clusters behind one API server. It was too complex and too fragile for real adoption, so it was archived. GitOps — where each cluster self-reconciles from Git — replaced it.

cards.title: Multi-Cluster Service Discovery
cards.teaser: When Service A lives in cluster-west and needs to reach Service B in cluster-east, CoreDNS in cluster-west cannot resolve it. Two projects solve this: the Kubernetes MCS API (a standard) and Submariner (an implementation). Understanding both is necessary to design cross-cluster routing.

runs.text: Standard Kubernetes services are cluster-scoped. A
is meaningless outside its cluster and a
allocates a cloud IP only in its home cluster. Two standards-track approaches address cross-cluster discovery:

items.text: The Multi-Cluster Services API introduces two new resource types:
. A service owner in cluster A creates a
to signal intent to share. An MCS controller creates a corresponding
in cluster B. CoreDNS in cluster B resolves the cross-cluster DNS name
and routes traffic to the endpoint in cluster A.

Submariner is a CNCF project that implements the MCS API and additionally provides an encrypted overlay network between clusters using WireGuard or IPsec. The Submariner Broker is a shared coordination plane (typically a dedicated cluster) that stores endpoint information. The Gateway Engine on each cluster establishes tunnels to peer clusters. Service endpoints in remote clusters appear as ECMP routes, enabling direct pod-to-pod connectivity across cluster boundaries.

runs.text: For teams not ready for a full Submariner deployment, a simpler pattern is

: expose inter-cluster services on public or private load balancers, register them in a shared DNS zone, and accept the extra hop. This is operationally simpler but does not provide encrypted tunnelling or IP-level routing.

Google's GKE Multi-Cluster Services and AWS's EKS cross-cluster service mesh both implement the MCS API. If you are on a managed Kubernetes platform, check whether your provider has a native MCS implementation before deploying Submariner.

The MCS API adds ServiceExport and ServiceImport to tell clusters about each other's services. Submariner implements that API and builds encrypted tunnels so pods in different clusters can talk directly. Together they make cross-cluster service calls look like local ones.

cards.title: GitOps: Git as the Cluster's Source of Truth
cards.teaser: GitOps inverts the push-based CI/CD model: instead of a pipeline pushing manifests into the cluster, the cluster continuously pulls its desired state from Git and reconciles toward it. This single inversion changes how drift is detected, how audits work, and how rollbacks happen.

runs.text: was coined by Weaveworks CEO Alexis Richardson in 2017. The core principle: the entire desired state of a Kubernetes cluster is stored in Git, and a controller running inside the cluster is the only thing that applies changes. No human — and no CI pipeline — runs
The four properties Weaveworks defined for a GitOps system:

items.text: The desired state of the system is expressed declaratively in Git (YAML manifests, Helm charts, Kustomize overlays). Procedures are not stored; outcomes are.
Git is an append-only log. Every change has an author, a timestamp, a diff, and a commit hash. Rollback is
The GitOps controller inside the cluster polls Git (or responds to webhooks) and applies approved state changes. No external system needs credentials to reach the cluster API server.
If the cluster drifts from the desired state — a pod is deleted, a ConfigMap is edited directly — the controller detects the deviation and corrects it on the next reconciliation cycle.

runs.text: The security model is a key benefit: the cluster never exposes its API server to external CI systems. The GitOps controller runs inside the cluster with a narrowly scoped service account. Credentials flow inward, not outward.

GitOps does not replace CI pipelines — CI still builds, tests, and pushes images. The boundary is the Git commit: CI produces the desired state; GitOps delivers it. A common pattern is for CI to open a PR that bumps an image tag in a Helm values file; a human (or automation) merges the PR; the GitOps controller then applies the change.

In GitOps, Git holds what the cluster should look like, and a controller inside the cluster continuously makes it so. You never run kubectl apply by hand — you commit to Git, and the cluster pulls the change itself.

cards.title: ArgoCD: Declarative GitOps for Kubernetes
cards.teaser: ArgoCD is the most widely adopted GitOps controller, originally built at Intuit to manage hundreds of applications across dozens of clusters. Its core abstraction — the Application CRD — maps a Git source to a cluster destination and continuously reconciles between them.

runs.text: ArgoCD was open-sourced by Intuit in 2018 and graduated as a CNCF project in 2022. Intuit runs it at scale: 1,500+ applications, 200+ clusters, managed by a small platform team. The architectural insight that made this scale possible: ArgoCD itself runs in Kubernetes and uses the Kubernetes API as its state store.

explanation.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: guestbook
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/argoproj/argocd-example-apps.git
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: guestbook
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: guestbook
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

items.text: — directory in the repo containing raw YAML, a Helm chart, or a Kustomize overlay. ArgoCD auto-detects the tool.
— the API server URL of the target cluster. For the cluster ArgoCD runs in, use
. Remote clusters are registered by URL and credentials.
— when true, ArgoCD reapplies Git state whenever live state diverges. When false, drift is reported but not corrected.
— when true, resources removed from Git are deleted from the cluster. Without prune, Git deletions are ignored (orphans accumulate).

runs.text: ArgoCD's UI provides a real-time diff view between desired state (Git) and live state (cluster), making it the primary operator interface for understanding deployment health. Every sync operation is recorded with the Git commit that triggered it.

ArgoCD supports multiple source types natively: raw YAML directories, Helm charts (local or from a registry), Kustomize overlays, and Jsonnet. The source type is auto-detected by the presence of Chart.yaml, kustomization.yaml, or neither.

ArgoCD watches a Git repo and continuously makes your cluster match it. You create an Application resource that says "this Git path should be deployed to this cluster namespace" and ArgoCD handles the rest — applying changes, healing drift, and pruning deleted resources.

cards.title: Flux: Multi-Tenant GitOps with Kustomize and Helm Native Support
cards.teaser: Flux is ArgoCD's main alternative, originated by Weaveworks (the company that coined GitOps). Flux v2 was rewritten from scratch using controller-runtime and a composable CRD model. Its multi-tenant design, source separation, and native Kustomize/Helm controllers differentiate it from ArgoCD.

runs.text: Flux v2 decomposes GitOps into small, composable controllers — the Source, Kustomize, Helm, Notification, and Image Automation controllers — each with its own CRD type. A minimal GitOps setup uses three resources:

explanation.text:
# 1. Source: tells Flux where Git lives
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata:
  name: flux-system
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1m
  url: https://github.com/my-org/my-fleet
  ref:
    branch: main
---
# 2. Kustomization: tells Flux what path to reconcile
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: apps
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 10m
  path: ./clusters/production
  prune: true
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: flux-system

runs.text: (reconciler) is intentional: many Kustomizations can reference the same GitRepository, and a single Kustomization can reference different sources. This composability is the foundation of Flux's multi-tenant model.

items.text: Each tenant gets a dedicated namespace and a dedicated GitRepository pointing to their own repo.
A platform team Kustomization in the
namespace provisions tenant namespaces and RBAC; tenant Kustomizations run with tenant service accounts.
field on a Kustomization impersonates a specific SA for reconciliation, enforcing least-privilege per tenant.

runs.text: CRD that manages a Helm release's lifecycle (install, upgrade, rollback) declaratively, triggered by Git changes to a

Flux breaks GitOps into small controllers: one fetches from Git, another applies Kustomize overlays, another manages Helm releases. Because each piece is separate, you can mix and match — one Git repo for platform config, another for each tenant's apps — all reconciled independently.

cards.title: ArgoCD vs Flux: A Side-by-Side Comparison
cards.teaser: ArgoCD and Flux are both mature, CNCF-graduated GitOps controllers used in large production deployments. Choosing between them is a product and team decision, not a correctness decision. The differences are in UI, multi-tenancy model, operational model, and extensibility.

runs.text: Both projects are CNCF Graduated (the highest maturity level) and have large production user bases. Key differences:

rows: UI
Built-in web UI with real-time diff, sync status, and history
No built-in UI; Weave GitOps (OSS) adds a UI; relies on CLI and Grafana
Primary abstraction
Application CRD (monolithic, one resource per app)
Composable CRDs: GitRepository + Kustomization / HelmRelease
Multi-tenancy
AppProject scopes repo and cluster access per team
Namespace-scoped Kustomizations with per-SA impersonation
Helm support
Helm as a source type inside Application; ArgoCD renders the templates
Dedicated HelmRelease + HelmRepository CRDs; Helm SDK native
Multi-cluster
ApplicationSet controller fans out to registered clusters
Each cluster runs its own Flux stack; fleet management via Git structure
Notification
Built-in webhook triggers; Notification CRD added later
Notification controller with Provider + Alert CRDs from day one
RBAC model
ArgoCD RBAC on top of Kubernetes RBAC (two layers)
Pure Kubernetes RBAC via service account impersonation
GitOps Bootstrap
argocd CLI or Helm install
flux bootstrap (generates and commits manifests to Git)

items.text: when you want a polished operator UI, a central control plane for multiple clusters, and a single Application resource per app. Teams that run manual sync workflows or need fine-grained sync windows benefit from ArgoCD's UI.

when you want strict multi-tenancy with Kubernetes-native RBAC, a fully GitOps-bootstrapped control plane (no UI to log into), or are building a platform that others deploy onto. Flux's composable model is more flexible for complex fleet structures.

runs.text: The projects are converging on a shared spec (OpenGitOps). Both support the Kubernetes-native pattern. Using either consistently and correctly produces better outcomes than using the wrong one perfectly — the tool matters less than the GitOps discipline.

ArgoCD gives you a rich web UI and a clean Application-per-app model; Flux gives you composable controllers and pure Kubernetes RBAC. Both get you to GitOps — ArgoCD is more operator-friendly, Flux is more platform-builder-friendly.

cards.title: Helm and Kustomize: Packaging vs Overlays
cards.teaser: Helm and Kustomize solve the same problem — "how do I deploy the same application to dev and prod with different config?" — with opposite philosophies. Helm is a templating engine; Kustomize is a patch overlay system. Knowing when to reach for each (and how to combine them) is a core GitOps skill.

runs.text: Helm was introduced with Kubernetes 1.2 as a package manager. A Helm chart is a directory containing a

explanation.text:
apiVersion: v2
name: my-service
description: A Helm chart for my-service
type: application
version: 1.4.2          # chart version
appVersion: "2.3.0"     # application image tag
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami

runs.text: at v1.14 and is available as
file to declare a base and a set of patches. No templates, no conditionals — just structural patches:

explanation.text:
# overlays/production/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../base
patchesStrategicMerge:
  - replica-patch.yaml
images:
  - name: my-service
    newTag: 2.3.0
configMapGenerator:
  - name: app-config
    literals:
      - ENV=production
      - LOG_LEVEL=warn

rows: Mechanism
Go template rendering + values substitution
JSON/strategic-merge patches on base manifests
Learning curve
Medium — Go template syntax, pipelines, helpers
Low — YAML patches mirror the object being patched
Conditionals
Yes (if/else in templates)
No — use multiple overlays instead
Distribution
Versioned chart packages in OCI registries
Git-native; no packaging step
Third-party charts
Vast public chart ecosystem (Artifact Hub)
Patch any chart or raw YAML; no chart required
Secret management
Values files may contain secrets — must be gitignored or encrypted
Patches must similarly avoid plaintext secrets
GitOps fit
Good with HelmRelease (Flux) or Helm source (ArgoCD)
Native — Kustomize overlays commit directly to Git

runs.text: A common production pattern: use a third-party Helm chart as a base and layer Kustomize patches on top of the rendered output. Both ArgoCD and Flux support this hybrid. The chart handles upstream defaults; Kustomize handles organisation-specific deviations.

Helm packages an app as a chart with Go templates and a values file — you swap out values per environment. Kustomize takes plain YAML and applies patches per environment — no templates, just surgical edits. Helm is better for distributing apps; Kustomize is better for org-specific overrides.

cards.title: App-of-Apps Pattern
cards.teaser: When you have 20 ArgoCD Applications to manage, you need something to manage them. The App-of-Apps pattern is a meta-application — an ArgoCD Application whose manifest directory contains other Application manifests. One sync bootstraps the whole fleet.

runs.text: The App-of-Apps pattern (popularised by ArgoCD, though Flux has an equivalent via Kustomization hierarchy) solves the bootstrapping problem: how do you get all your Application resources into the cluster without applying them one by one?
The root application points at a directory that contains nothing but other Application manifests:

explanation.text:
# Root application — points at the apps/ directory
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: root
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/my-org/my-fleet
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: argocd
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

runs.text: , and each microservice. The root application syncs and creates all children. Each child then reconciles its own source independently.

items.text: Bootstrapping a new cluster requires only: install ArgoCD + apply the root Application. Everything else self-provisions.
The ArgoCD UI shows one tree: root → child applications → workload resources. Sync status and health are visible at every level.
Each child application can have its own sync policy (automated or manual), sync windows, and health thresholds.

runs.text: references subdirectories that each contain their own Kustomization or HelmRelease resources. The reconciliation tree is the same; the CRD types differ.

Avoid deep nesting (root → platform → infra → app). Three levels is typically the maximum before debugging a failed sync becomes a game of tracing parent-child relationships. Keep the tree shallow and the dependency ordering explicit.

App-of-Apps is an ArgoCD Application that manages other ArgoCD Applications. You apply one root app to a fresh cluster and it bootstraps the entire fleet — every service, every infrastructure component — by creating child apps that each reconcile independently.

cards.title: Drift Detection
cards.teaser: Drift is when what is running in the cluster no longer matches what is declared in Git. It can happen from emergency hotfixes applied directly with kubectl, from operators that mutate resources, or from external systems. Detecting and responding to drift is where GitOps earns its operational value.

runs.text: Drift is inevitable in any cluster touched by humans. The sources:

items.text: An on-call engineer scales a Deployment from 3 to 10 replicas during an incident. The edit resolves the incident but is never committed to Git. The cluster now has more replicas than Git says it should.
A cluster autoscaler, a VPA, or a cert-manager controller mutates a resource field after ArgoCD last applied it. ArgoCD will see those fields as differing from Git.
Mutating webhooks (Istio sidecars, pod security injectors) add fields to resources that were not in the original Git manifest.

runs.text: status on the Application. The diff view shows each field that differs. Flux reports drift in the
status conditions and via the Notification controller.
rules that exclude specific fields from drift calculation:

explanation.text:
spec:
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas           # managed by HPA
    - group: ""
      kind: Secret
      managedFieldsManagers:
        - cert-manager-controller  # cert-manager owns this secret

runs.text: Flux uses server-side apply field ownership: because Flux applies with
, fields owned by other managers (HPA, VPA) are not overwritten on reconciliation. This is structurally cleaner than ArgoCD's ignore list but requires Kubernetes 1.22+ with SSA stable.

The most dangerous drift is drift that nobody knows about. A GitOps controller with alerting disabled, or with selfHeal set to false and no one watching the sync status dashboard, provides no protection against drift accumulating silently over weeks.

Drift is the gap between what Git says and what the cluster is running. ArgoCD flags it as OutOfSync; Flux detects it on each reconciliation cycle. The controller can either alert on drift or automatically heal it — but either way you have to watch the signals.

cards.title: Auto-Sync vs Manual Sync
cards.teaser: Auto-sync means the GitOps controller applies every committed change without human intervention. Manual sync means a human reviews and approves before anything is applied. The right policy depends on the environment, the blast radius, and the maturity of the test suite — and most real fleets use both.

runs.text: ; Flux: all Kustomizations reconcile automatically by design) gives you the full GitOps benefit: commit to Git, cluster catches up within the polling interval (typically 1–10 minutes). No human is in the loop between a git push and a running pod.
Manual sync preserves a human gate. In ArgoCD, removing
when Git changes but does not apply. An operator must press "Sync" in the UI or run

Sync windows (ArgoCD) and suspended Kustomizations (Flux) provide a middle ground: auto-sync is enabled but constrained to a time window (e.g., only during business hours, never during the peak trading period).

rows: Auto-sync + self-heal
Dev, staging, non-critical prod; high test confidence
Bad commit auto-deploys before anyone notices
Auto-sync, no self-heal
Prod where you want Git changes applied but not drift-healed
Drift from operators accumulates; still auto-applies bad commits
Manual sync
Regulated environments; prod with low deploy frequency; when releases require approval
Stale environments; human bottleneck; sync debt accumulates
Sync window
Prod where deploy timing matters (maintenance windows, trading hours)
Commits queue up; large batched changes at window open

runs.text: uses auto-sync without self-heal (so Git changes deploy, but operator mutations are not overwritten), with a sync window during the deployment hours.

Regulated industries (SOC 2, PCI DSS) typically require a documented approval for production changes. Auto-sync satisfies this if the Git PR merge is the approval record. The PR merge timestamp, the approver's identity, and the diff are all stored in Git history — this is often sufficient for audit.

Auto-sync means every Git commit immediately becomes a running change — fast but risky without a good test gate. Manual sync adds a human approval step before anything is applied — safe but slow. Most teams auto-sync dev and staging, and use manual sync or sync windows for production.

cards.title: Environment Promotion via Git PRs
cards.teaser: GitOps environment promotion means that promoting a release from dev to staging to production is a Git operation, not a CLI command. A PR bumps an image tag in the production values file; merging the PR is the deployment. The entire history of who deployed what, when, and with what change is in Git.

runs.text: The canonical GitOps promotion pattern separates application source repos from environment configuration repos (or directories):

items.text: — source code + Dockerfile. CI builds and pushes an image tagged with the commit SHA (e.g.,
— Kustomize overlays or Helm values files per environment. A directory structure like
holds the image tag for each environment.
. CI also opens a PR against the config repo that sets
The dev PR is auto-merged (or merged by the developer). The GitOps controller deploys to dev within minutes.
After dev tests pass, a separate PR is opened (manually or by automation) targeting
After staging sign-off, a production PR is opened targeting
. This PR requires an approver. Merging it is the production deployment.

runs.text: controller that can automate step 1: it watches an OCI registry, detects a new tag matching a semver policy, and opens a Git commit or PR with the bumped tag. ArgoCD relies on external tooling (Argo CD Image Updater, or a CI step) for the same purpose.

The Git PR is the deployment record. Who approved it, what changed, what tests ran on the PR — all of this is in the Git log. This satisfies change-management audit requirements for SOC 2, ISO 27001, and most financial regulators without additional tooling.

GitOps promotion is simple: CI builds an image and bumps its tag in a values file via a PR. Each environment has its own values file. Merging the PR for the prod values file is the production deployment. Git history is the deployment log.

cards.title: ApplicationSet: GitOps at Fleet Scale
cards.teaser: ArgoCD's ApplicationSet controller generates Application resources dynamically from a template and a generator — a cluster list, a Git directory tree, or a matrix of both. One ApplicationSet definition can manage the same application across 50 clusters without 50 separate Application manifests.

runs.text: is a CRD introduced in ArgoCD v2.0 (previously a standalone project). It solves the fleet-scale problem: if you have 20 clusters and want to deploy the same workload to all of them, you do not want 20 separate Application YAML files.
A minimal ApplicationSet using the Cluster generator:

explanation.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: guestbook
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  generators:
    - clusters:
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            env: production
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "guestbook-{{.name}}"
    spec:
      project: default
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/my-org/guestbook
        targetRevision: main
        path: helm
        helm:
          valueFiles:
            - values.yaml
            - "values-{{.metadata.labels.region}}.yaml"
      destination:
        server: "{{.server}}"
        namespace: guestbook
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true

runs.text: When a new cluster is registered in ArgoCD with the
label, the ApplicationSet controller automatically generates a new Application for it. No manual manifest required.

items.text: — creates one Application per directory matching a glob in the source repo. Used for monorepo structures where each subdirectory is an app.
— cross-product of two generators (e.g., all apps × all clusters = one Application per app-cluster pair).
— creates a temporary Application per open PR for preview environments. ArgoCD deletes the Application when the PR closes.

runs.text: Flux's equivalent pattern is a Kustomization in the platform namespace that references a directory containing per-cluster or per-tenant subdirectories. The structure is the generator; Flux reconciles everything it finds. Less dynamic than ApplicationSet generators but equally powerful for static fleet configurations.

ApplicationSet is a template for ArgoCD Applications. Instead of writing one Application manifest per cluster, you write one ApplicationSet that says "generate an Application for every cluster labelled production." Add a new cluster label and the app deploys automatically.
